title: Daswandh, in practice
hookLine: set aside a tenth, or start with less
tomorrow: Simran's tenth is in the envelope. where should it actually go?

cards: Bebe Jaswant keeps a jar on the windowsill beside her chili plants, folded bills and coins, and nobody in the family is allowed to borrow from it. Ever. Simran always assumed it was for emergencies.
On Sunday Bebe hands her an empty envelope with one word written on it in Gurmukhi. For your first pay, she says. A tenth goes in before you buy anything.
Simran does the math on her phone and makes a face.

teach.b: The word on the envelope is daswandh: a tenth share of what you earn, set aside for others. The Granth asks for a share.
On ang 1245, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: one who eats what he earns by his own work, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path.
Sikh tradition names the share as a tenth, given through the gurdwara or straight to people who need it.
Then Bebe adds the honest part, the part Simran's face was asking for: if a tenth is too much right now, start with less. Put something in, and let it grow.
And look how the whole week lands in that envelope. Clean work earned the money. Fair weights kept every bag honest.
Work as seva shaped how the hours were spent. Faith at work came along for every shift, clinking on the scale. Deal fairly made sure each dollar was really hers.
And enough left room for the envelope at all. Daswandh is where six lines turn into something you can hold. Simran folds a bill inside, then one more, and licks the flap.

how: Sikh families set aside daswandh from their earnings and give it through the gurdwara or directly to people and causes in need; some begin with a smaller share.

games.why: a tenth if you can, less to begin. Simran folded in a bill, then one more, from her first pay.

practice: Set something aside right now, however small: a coin in a cup, a bill in a drawer, a note in your phone that says this part is for someone else. Then sit, and let it stay there, already given away in your mind.
